newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor radiation leak at Japan nuclear plant.
newsitem.headline: Minor radiation leak at Japan nuclear plant.

text.p: A new reactor at the world's largest nuclear power plant in northern Japan developed a minor radiation leak on Friday but the problem was quickly solved and no one was exposed to radiation, a spokesman for its operator Tokyo Electric Power Co (TEPCO) said.
The spokesman told Reuters on Saturday there was also no leakage of radiation outside the facility itself and no disruption to operations at the plant.

Vapour containing a small amount of radioactive substance leaked at around 9:30 a.m. (0030 GMT) on Friday from a gauge inside the unit that houses the turbine of the No. 7 reactor at the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa atomic power plant in Niigata Prefecture along the Sea of Japan coast.

"At 9.20 a.m. on Friday morning radioactive steam was discovered leaking from a pressure gauge on turbine seven. We estimate less than three litres of radioactive steam escaped from the gauge. No one was exposed to radiation and no radiation leaked outside the facility," spokesman Hakuei Shinoda said.
"The amount of radioactivity released was around 370 becquerels, which is equivalent to the natural background radiation found in a 10 kg (5 lb) bag of rice."
The incident was the first ever radioactivity leak since the Kashiwazaki nuclear plant, some 200 km (125 miles) northwest of Tokyo, went into operation in 1978.

The No. 7 reactor, with an output capacity of 1,355,600 kilowatts, went into operation on a commercial basis early this month, making the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant the world's largest nuclear plant in terms of overall power generation.
The plant is capable of producing 8.21 million kilowatts when all seven of its reactors are in operation.
A Canadian nuclear power station was previously the world's largest with an output capacity of some 7.3 million kilowatts.
It was not the first time the No. 7 reactor, an advanced boiling-water one, had run into problems.
Trial runs of the reactor were held up for about 10 days in May when a tube to measure turbine pressure burst.
Tadao Yabe, a Kashiwazaki municipal assemblyman who opposes the nuclear power plant, said the leak and delay in reporting the accident until Saturday was "quite shocking."
"Tokyo Electric Power should report any minor accidents. This .... goes to show the safety of the No. 7 reactor has not been adequately proven," he told Kyodo News Service
Japan's nuclear power programme has been under fire in recent months because of a series of accidents and coverup of incidents at nuclear plants.

On Friday, Japan's state-run nuclear power company announced disciplinary measures against 24 company officials for the cover-up of an accident which occurred at one of its nuclear plants 18 months ago.
Prototype fast-breeder reactor Monju, operated by the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) on the Sea of Japan coast, was the scene of a massive sodium coolant leak in December 1995.

A PNC spokesman said that four senior company officials, including vice president Tadayoshi Suda, and 20 other company employees would be punished through a one-month suspension or a salary cut, among other measures.
